fields.h1: How to Have Assurance of Salvation
fields.meta_title: How to Have Assurance of Salvation — And Know You're Saved
fields.description: Can you actually know you're saved? Here is what the Bible says about assurance of salvation, where real confidence comes from, and what to do with doubt.
fields.body_html:
“How can I know I’m really saved?” It is one of the most anxious questions a Christian can ask, and one of the most common. You believe — and then you sin, or you doubt, or the feelings fade, and the old fear returns: what if it isn’t real? What if, in the end, I am not actually his?

The good news is that God does not mean for his children to live in that fear. Assurance — the settled confidence that you belong to Christ — is not presumption or wishful thinking. It is something God wants you to have. Here is where it comes from, and what to do when doubt creeps back in.

God wants you to know

Start with this, because it changes everything: the Bible was written, in part, precisely so that believers could be sure. John says so plainly: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). Not hope, not guess — know. Assurance is not spiritual arrogance; it is the normal, intended experience of a child of God, and God has gone out of his way to make it available. A child does not lie awake each night wondering whether they still belong to their family; the relationship is settled, and they rest in it. God means for his children to rest in theirs.

Where assurance is NOT found

Much of our trouble comes from looking for assurance in the wrong place: in the strength of our feelings, or the consistency of our performance. But feelings rise and fall with sleep and weather, and no honest Christian can rest their confidence on their own record. That is why John Wesley, in his sermon The Almost Christian, warned so sharply against a religion that has the outward form but has never truly rested on Christ — a sincerity that is real as far as it goes but has not gone all the way to the Savior. Assurance built on our own goodness will always wobble, because our goodness always wobbles. On a day of obedience we feel saved; on a day of failure we feel lost — and our confidence rides up and down like a boat on the tide, because it is anchored to the wrong thing. A faith that looks mainly at itself will always find reasons to doubt, because it is looking at a sinner. The cure is not to try harder to feel assured, but to look away from ourselves altogether, to the One who saves.

Where assurance is found: the finished work of Christ

Real assurance rests not on how well we are holding on to God but on how securely he is holding on to us. Jesus said of his sheep, “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:28–29). Two hands, and yours is not one of them. Your security is not your grip on Christ but his grip on you.

This was Charles Spurgeon’s great theme. In All of Grace he pleads the anxious inquirer away from themselves and back to the cross again and again: salvation is God’s free gift, received by faith, resting entirely on what Christ has done. And Jesus gave the doubter a promise to stand on: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). If you have come, he has not cast you out — he has said he never will. Paul was so sure of this that he could write, “I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me” (2 Timothy 1:12). Note where his confidence lay: not in himself, but in the One he had believed.

When your own heart condemns you

Sometimes the loudest voice against our assurance is not the devil or the world but our own conscience. We look inward, see our sin and coldness, and our heart passes sentence: someone like you cannot really be saved. John knew this experience, and he answers it with one of the most comforting sentences in Scripture: “we shall reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:19–20). Read that again slowly. When your heart condemns you, God is greater than your heart. He knows every sin your conscience is accusing you of — and he sent his Son to die for exactly those, and he still calls you his child. Your heart is not the highest court. God is, and in Christ his verdict over the believing sinner is not condemnation but acceptance.

This does not mean we silence conscience or excuse sin; a conscience troubled by real sin should drive us to repentance. But it means we do not let a condemning heart have the final word about our standing with God. That word belongs to Christ, and to the finished work he accomplished on the cross — a work that does not become less finished on our worst days.

The witness of the Spirit and the marks of new life

God gives two further supports to our assurance. The first is inward: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16). There is a quiet, God-given confidence the Spirit works in a believing heart — not a feeling we manufacture, but a witness he gives. The second is the evidence of changed life. John points to it: “We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers” (1 John 3:14). A genuine faith produces, however imperfectly, new desires, new grief over sin, a new love for God’s people. These are not the ground of our assurance — Christ alone is that — but they are its confirmation, the fruit that shows the root is alive.

What to do with doubt

John Bunyan, who wrote Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, spent years tormented by doubt about his own salvation before he came to rest. His story is a gift to every struggler, because it shows that assurance is often not a single sunrise but a hard-won dawn. If doubt assails you:

  • Preach the promises to yourself. Do not argue with your feelings on their own terms; answer them with God’s word — John 6:37, 1 John 5:13, John 10:28.
  • Look to Christ, not to your looking. Assurance grows as you gaze at the Savior, not as you inspect the quality of your own faith.
  • Keep coming. The evidence of true faith is that it keeps returning to Christ, even after failure. A dead faith stays away; a living one comes back.
  • Give doubt time, and give it to God. Assurance often grows the way confidence in any love grows — not by one grand proof but by a long history of faithfulness. Bunyan did not reason his way to peace in an afternoon; he came to rest as he kept returning to the promises until they held.

It is worth adding that a measure of doubt is not proof of a false faith — often it is the mark of a tender conscience that takes God seriously. The presumptuous rarely worry whether they are saved; it is those who long to be Christ’s who fear they might not be. If that is you, take heart: the very anxiety you feel about your soul is evidence you care for the God you fear you have missed — and he does not despise a soul that wants him.

And rest here, finally: “I am sure that neither death nor life … nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). The One who began a good work in you “will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). Your salvation was never resting on your strength. It rests on his — and he will not let go.

So if you are in Christ, hear this and let your heart rest: you are not more saved on your best day or less saved on your worst. You were saved by grace, you are kept by grace, and you will be brought home by grace. Assurance is not the reward for a flawless life; it is the birthright of a child who has learned where to look. Stop staring at the storm and the strength of your own grip, and fix your eyes on the Savior who holds you. He caught you when you first came. He has not dropped you since. And he has promised, in words that cannot fail, that he never will.
